'''Emmanuel David Tannenbaum''' ({{Langx|he|עמנואל דוד טננבאום}}; June 28, 1978 – May 28, 2012)<ref name="chem" /> was an [[Israel]]i/American biophysicist and applied mathematician. He worked as a professor and researcher in the department of chemistry at the [[Ben-Gurion University of the Negev]] and the department of biology at the [[Georgia Institute of Technology]], specializing in the fields of [[mathematical biology]], [[systems biology]], and [[quantum physics]].

Tannenbaum's initial work was in quantum chemistry as part of his [[Harvard University]] doctoral thesis<ref name="Tannenbaum-thesis"/> where he developed a novel [[partial differential equation]] approach to the [[Einstein–Brillouin–Keller method|EBK quantization]] of nearly separable Hamiltonians in the quasi-integrable regime. Emmanuel Tannenbaum subsequently devoted his research to studying various problems in [[evolutionary dynamics]] using [[Quasispecies model|quasispecies]] models.<ref name="Tannenbaum-quasispecies"/> His seminal work centered on the key question of the evolutionary advantages of [[sexual reproduction]]. Tannenbaum demonstrated a strong selective advantage for [[sexual reproduction]] with fewer and much less restrictive assumptions than previously considered.<ref>Choosing Sex Is a Matter of Time (E.D. Tannenbaum's featured work at American Physical Society) http://psychcentral.com/news/archives/2006-03/aps-bpm012706.html {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140223022020/http://psychcentral.com/news/archives/2006-03/aps-bpm012706.html |date=2014-02-23 }}</ref> Closely related to this line of reasoning, was the original work by Tannenbaum and James Sherley on the [[Immortal DNA strand hypothesis|immortal strand hypothesis]]. Tannenbaum also proposed a pioneering theory of why higher organisms need sleep.<ref>Michael Schirber, APS Focus: "Why sleep?" (An account of E.D. Tannenbaum's work on the theory of sleep) http://physics.aps.org/story/v21/st1</ref> Towards the end of his life, he proposed a new approach to anti-[[stealth technology]] based on the theory of [[Bose–Einstein condensate]].<ref>Stealth Technology: E.D. Tannenbaum. {{ArXiv|1208.2377}}</ref>

Emmanuel Tannenbaum received a number of honors, including the [[Robert Karplus]] Prize in Chemical Physics from [[Harvard University]], the prestigious [[Alon Fellowship]]<ref>The Alon Fellowship. {{cite web |url=http://che.org.il/en/?page_id=9062 |title=Allon Fellowships for Outstanding Young Researchers &#124; the Council for Higher Education of Israel |access-date=2012-12-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130129235935/http://che.org.il/en/?page_id=9062 |archive-date=2013-01-29 }}</ref> from the [[Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities]], and a [[National Institutes of Health]] research fellowship.<ref>National Institutes of Health Fellowship: E.D. Tannenbaum (Harvard University). https://report.nih.gov/award/index.cfm?ot=&fy=2005&state=&ic=NIGMS&fm=&orgid=3212901&distr=&rfa=&view=data&pil=T#tabpi</ref> Dr. Tannenbaum is the son of mathematician [[Allen Tannenbaum]] and chemist [[Rina Tannenbaum]]. His sister, Sarah Tannenbaum-Dvir, is an oncologist/hematologist.{{citation needed|date=August 2022}}
